reason: Ninlil is literally the Sumerian 'Lady of the Wind' (𒀭𒊩𒌆𒆤); her domain is the moving air that turbines harvest.
Wind carries pollen across fields and ripples through grain; Ninlil's cult at Nippur sat at the heart of Mesopotamian agrarian society, and her son Enbilulu oversees canals and abundance.
As goddess of the air, Ninlil personifies the atmosphere and the breath that links sky, land, and living things.
The Sumerian poem Enlil and Ninlil (ETCSL 1.2.1) and temple hymns from Nippur make her a key figure in the reconstructed archive of Mesopotamian religion.
